chunks: Do you not see that Allāh, the Glorified, has tried all the people among those who came before, beginning with Adam, upto the last ones in this world with stones which yield neither benefit nor harm, which neither see nor hear. He made those stones into His sacred house which He made a standby for the people.

He placed it in the most rugged stony part of the earth and on a highland with least soil thereon, among the most narrow valleys between rough mountains, soft sandy plains, springs of scanty water and scattered habitants, where neither camels nor horses nor cows and sheep can prosper.

key_terms.أَوْعَرِ بِقَاعِ الْأَرْضِ: The most rugged/stony part of the earth
key_terms.الْآخِرِينَ: The last ones (people of the later ages)
key_terms.الْأَوَّلِينَ: The first ones (early prophets and peoples)

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the Ka'bah's location according to Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) uses the metaphor of 'stones that neither hurt nor benefit' to illustrate God's testing of humanity through the Ka'bah, emphasizing that its sanctity is derived from divine decree rather than geographical or material grandeur. This passage, found in the sermon 'Al-Qasaa'', serves as a critique of worldly vanity by contrasting the Ka'bah's humble, arid location in the barren valley of Mecca with its exalted spiritual status, reminding believers that true worth lies in piety, not physical attributes.
